overview.title: Why scaling hasn't fixed the limits
overview.main_topic: The argument that scaling laws measure memorization and that scaling cannot fix the fundamental problems of deep learning; start of the comparison between deep learning and biological intelligence
overview.central_idea: Scaling laws show predictable gains on benchmarks that are effectively memorization tests; they say nothing about adaptation to novelty, oversensitivity to phrasing or learning generalizable programs, which are inherent to curve fitting. Since models are still parametric curves fitted by gradient descent with Transformers, these problems remain despite four to five orders of magnitude of scaling.
overview.importance: This is the pivot of the chapter: it closes the list of limitations by arguing they are structural, which is the premise for the search for new approaches in sections 19.3 and 19.4.
learning_objectives: State what scaling laws are and what evidence they provide
Explain the book's critique that benchmarks used in scaling-law arguments are memorization tests
List the three fundamental problems scaling won't solve and relate each to 19.1.1-19.1.3
Explain the distinction introduced in 19.2.1 between a differentiable parametric function and the human brain
prerequisites: LLM scaling trends and the GPT family (chapter 16, p.529-530)
Gradient descent and the Transformer architecture

summary:
The page continues the 'scale is all you need' story: in early 2023 GPT-4 had just been released, "essentially a scaled-up version of GPT-3: more parameters, more training data." Its much better performance suggested you could keep going to a GPT-5 that would be more of the same and from which AGI would spontaneously emerge.

Proponents cite **scaling laws**: empirical relationships between model size (and dataset size) and performance on specific tasks, suggesting that bigger models reliably and predictably perform better. The author's objection: the benchmarks used to measure "performance" are effectively **memorization tests**, like university exams. LLMs do well on them by memorizing answers, so cramming more questions and answers into bigger models naturally improves scores.

Scaling has not produced progress on the issues of section 19.1 (inability to adapt to novelty, oversensitivity to phrasing, inability to infer generalizable programs for reasoning problems) because they are **inherent to curve fitting**, the paradigm of deep learning. The author says he started pointing these out in 2017 and they persist with models four or five orders of magnitude larger, because *the models we're using are still the same*: parametric curves fitted via gradient descent, using the Transformer, for over seven years.

Scaling by adding layers and data won't solve three fundamental problems:
1. Models are limited to **interpolative programs memorized at training time** and can't synthesize new programs at inference time for substantially novel situations.
2. Even in known situations, these programs **generalize poorly**, causing oversensitivity to phrasing and confounder features.
3. Models are **limited in what they can represent**: most programs can't be expressed as a continuous geometric morphing of a data manifold, especially algorithmic reasoning.

Section **19.2.1, Automatons vs. intelligent agents**, begins: deep learning's geometric morphing from input to output differs fundamentally from how humans think and learn, not only because humans learn from embodied experience rather than explicit examples, but because the brain is "an entirely different beast compared to a differentiable parametric function."

paragraphs.excerpt: been released, and it was essentially a scaled-up version of GPT-3: more parameters,
paragraphs.what_it_says: GPT-4 had just been released and was essentially a scaled-up GPT-3: more parameters, more training data. Its much better performance suggested that you could keep going to a GPT-5 that would be more of the same and from which AGI would spontaneously emerge.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The inference being described is extrapolation: a big jump from GPT-3 to GPT-4 by scaling suggests further jumps by further scaling, possibly all the way to general intelligence. The word 'spontaneously' captures the belief that no new ideas would be needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the hypothesis the section tests. The rest of the page argues that the extrapolation confuses improvement on memorization benchmarks with progress toward intelligence.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book's text here): OpenAI did not publish GPT-4's architecture or size, as chapter 16 also notes (p.529). 'Scaled-up GPT-3' is the author's characterization of what was publicly understood, not a disclosed specification.

terminology.meaning: AI with human-level general ability to learn and adapt across tasks.

connections: p.594: start of the sentence and of section 19.2.
p.529: Figure 16.8 on LLM parameter counts and dataset sizes; GPT-4 details undisclosed.

paragraphs.excerpt: Proponents of this view would point to “scaling laws” as evidence. Scaling laws
paragraphs.what_it_says: Proponents cite scaling laws: an empirical relationship between model size (and training-set size) and performance on specific tasks, suggesting larger models reliably and predictably perform better. But the benchmarks used to measure performance are effectively memorization tests, like those given to university students. LLMs do well by memorizing answers, and putting more questions and answers into the models naturally improves performance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The critique does not deny that scaling laws hold. It questions what they measure. If a benchmark rewards knowing answers, bigger models with more data store more answers and score better, in a smooth, predictable way. That is evidence of better memorization, not of better adaptation.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a lesson in evaluation: a metric's trend is only as meaningful as what the metric tests. To measure progress toward intelligence, you need tests that can't be passed by memorization (the motivation for ARC, p.605).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: published scaling laws (e.g. Kaplan et al. 2020, Hoffmann et al. 2022) relate model and data size mostly to the *pretraining loss* (next-token prediction), which in turn correlates with many benchmark scores. See the math section.

terminology.meaning: Empirical relationships, typically power laws, between model size, dataset size or compute and performance.
A test that can be passed by recalling stored answers or patterns rather than adapting to something new.

connections: p.529: chapter 16: more compute generally leads to better LLM performance, no asymptote yet in next-token prediction.
p.605: ARC Prize, a benchmark designed to resist memorization.

paragraphs.excerpt: The reality is that scaling up our models hasn’t led to any progress
paragraphs.what_it_says: Scaling has not led to progress on the issues listed (inability to adapt to novelty, oversensitivity to phrasing, inability to infer generalizable programs for reasoning problems), because they are inherent to curve fitting, the paradigm of deep learning. The author says he pointed out these problems in 2017 and they persist with models four or five orders of magnitude larger and more knowledgeable. No progress has been made because the models are still the same: parametric curves fitted to a dataset via gradient descent, using the Transformer architecture, for over seven years.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Scaling changes the quantity (more parameters, more data) but not the kind of model. If a limitation follows from the kind (a static fitted curve), more of the same can't remove it. Being 'more knowledgeable' (more stored content) is distinct from being better at handling the new.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the central claim of section 19.2: progress on these problems requires a change in paradigm, not size, which motivates the 'test-time adaptation' and program-synthesis discussions later (p.606, p.613).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: four to five orders of magnitude means a factor of 10,000 to 100,000 in model size or compute between 2017-era models and current frontier LLMs. The Transformer was introduced in 2017 ('Attention Is All You Need').

terminology.meaning: Adjusting the parameters of a function so it fits a dataset; the book's description of what deep learning does.

connections: p.630: chapter 20: five years of scaling base LLMs haven't overcome these constraints; the shift to test-time adaptation.

paragraphs.excerpt: Scaling up current deep learning techniques by stacking more layers and using more
paragraphs.what_it_says: Scaling up current techniques (more layers, more training data) won't solve the fundamental problems of deep learning, listed in the bullets that follow.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sentence introduces a summary of section 19.1 restated as structural limits.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the three-item list that is the most compact statement of the book's critique.

paragraphs.excerpt: Deep-learning models are limited to using interpolative programs they memorize at training time.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models are limited to interpolative programs memorized at training time. They can't, on their own, synthesize brand-new programs at inference time to adapt to substantially novel situations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This restates 19.1.1. A program can be combined or interpolated with others, but nothing new is created when a new situation arrives, since parameters are frozen at inference time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: 'On their own' and 'at inference time' are precise qualifiers: the chapter later discusses test-time adaptation, where search or fine-tuning happens during inference (p.606), which targets exactly this limitation.

terminology.meaning: Generating a new program to solve a task (discussed in section 19.4.4, p.613).

connections: p.589: 19.1.1, deep learning models struggle to adapt to novelty.
p.613: program synthesis as an alternative approach.

paragraphs.excerpt: Even within known situations, these interpolative programs suffer from generalization issues, which
paragraphs.what_it_says: Even in known situations, these interpolative programs have generalization issues, which lead to oversensitivity to phrasing and to confounder features.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This restates 19.1.2. A confounder feature is something correlated with the right answer in training data but not causally related to it (names, wording, image textures). The programs depend on such features, so changing them changes the output.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects prompt sensitivity and adversarial examples to a single cause: the learned programs are approximations tied to the specific training distribution.

terminology.meaning: An input feature that correlates with the target in the training data but isn't what determines it, so relying on it causes errors elsewhere.

connections: p.592: the Alice riddle and prompt engineering.
p.594: models take any shortcut available to fit their training data.

paragraphs.excerpt: Deep learning models are limited in what they can represent, and most of
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models are limited in what they can represent: most programs you might want to learn can't be expressed as a continuous geometric morphing of a data manifold, particularly algorithmic reasoning tasks. A transition sentence then announces a closer look at what separates biological intelligence from deep learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This restates 19.1.3: a fitted continuous transform suits perception but not exact discrete procedures like addition with carries.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Unlike the first two, this is a limit on representation, not just learning, so more data can't remove it. The transition sets up the comparison with brains in 19.2.1.

terminology.term: Geometric morphing of a data manifold
terminology.meaning: The book's description of what a network computes: a continuous deformation that maps the input data manifold onto the target space.

connections: p.593: digit addition and the 'static chain of continuous geometric transformations'.
p.612: why deep learning isn't a complete answer to abstraction generation.

paragraphs.excerpt: There are fundamental differences between the straightforward geometric morphing from input to output
paragraphs.what_it_says: There are fundamental differences between deep learning's geometric morphing from input to output and how humans think and learn. It's not just that humans learn from embodied experience rather than explicit training examples; the brain is an entirely different beast compared to a differentiable parametric function.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The section moves from 'what deep learning can't do' to 'how biological intelligence works differently'. The title contrasts automatons (fixed input-to-output machines) with intelligent agents (which adapt). The next page argues from evolution that brains began as stores of hardcoded behavioral programs, like insect brains.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the central concept of the chapter: intelligence as the ability to adapt to novelty, not just to execute stored programs, which leads to local vs. extreme generalization (p.597).

terminology.meaning: A system that executes fixed behavior in response to inputs, without adapting it.
A function with tunable parameters whose output can be differentiated with respect to them; what a neural network is.

connections: p.596: brains as evolutionary adaptations storing behavioral programs; the C. elegans brain network (Figure 19.5).

concepts.name: Scaling laws
concepts.definition: Empirical relationships between model size (and dataset size) and performance on specific tasks, suggesting predictable improvement as models grow.
concepts.intuition: Plot performance against model size on log axes and you get a smooth trend.
concepts.technical: Typically power laws in parameters, data or compute for pretraining loss (beyond the book: Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022).
concepts.significance: The main evidence cited for 'scale is all you need'; the book argues they measure memorization benchmarks.
concepts.example: GPT-3 to GPT-4: more parameters and data, much better benchmark performance.
concepts.misconception: That predictable gains on benchmarks imply progress toward general intelligence.

concepts.name: 'Scale is all you need'
concepts.definition: The view that making models bigger and training them on more data will overcome deep learning's limitations and lead to general intelligence.
concepts.intuition: If bigger has always been better, keep making it bigger.
concepts.technical: Extrapolates scaling-law trends; assumes AGI would emerge from more of the same.
concepts.significance: Rejected in section 19.2 because the limitations are inherent to curve fitting.
concepts.example: The expectation of a GPT-5 'more of the same' from which AGI would emerge.
concepts.misconception: That becoming more knowledgeable is the same as becoming better at adapting.

concepts.name: Deep learning as curve fitting
concepts.definition: Deep learning fits parametric curves (functions with many parameters) to datasets via gradient descent.
concepts.intuition: Bending a flexible surface until it passes through all your data points.
concepts.technical: Parameters are learned at training time and frozen at inference; the result is a continuous map between vector spaces.
concepts.significance: The book traces all three fundamental problems to this paradigm, which has not changed in over seven years.
concepts.example: Transformers trained by gradient descent on next-token prediction.
concepts.misconception: That bigger curves stop being curves.

concepts.name: Automaton vs. intelligent agent
concepts.definition: An automaton executes fixed input-to-output behavior; an intelligent agent adapts its behavior to new situations.
concepts.intuition: A vending machine vs. a person who figures out what to do when the machine is broken.
concepts.technical: Deep learning models, as fixed differentiable functions at inference time, are closer to automatons.
concepts.significance: Introduced in 19.2.1 and developed with the evolution of brains on the next page.
concepts.example: Insect brains executing hardcoded behavioral programs (p.596).

concepts.name: Confounder features
concepts.definition: Features correlated with the target in the training data that don't actually determine it.
concepts.intuition: Learning that 'answers in bold are correct' from a badly made exam.
concepts.technical: Interpolative programs pick up such features, leading to sensitivity to irrelevant changes.
concepts.significance: Part of the second fundamental problem in the list.
concepts.example: Names in a riddle, background texture in an image.
concepts.misconception: That a feature useful on the training set is relevant to the task.

math.title: Typical form of a scaling law (not in the book)
math.source_text: Scaling laws are an empirical relationship observed between the size of a deep learning model (as well as the size of its training dataset) and its performance on specific tasks.

variables.meaning: Test loss (for LLMs, usually the next-token cross-entropy) of a model with N parameters trained with enough data
A fitted constant setting the scale
A fitted exponent, small (around 0.076 in Kaplan et al. 2020)

math.operations: A power law: loss decreases by a constant factor each time N is multiplied by a constant factor, which appears as a straight line on log-log axes.
math.purpose: Gives a concrete form to the book's verbal description of scaling laws. The book gives no formula; this is the standard form from the literature.
math.interpretation: Gains are predictable but diminishing in absolute terms. The book's critique is not about the form of the curve but about what the measured quantity tests: memorization-heavy loss and benchmarks.
math.intuition: Each tenfold increase in size buys the same proportional improvement.
math.numerical_example: With $\alpha_N = 0.076$, multiplying $N$ by 10 multiplies the loss by $10^{-0.076} \approx 0.84$, a 16% reduction. Going up four orders of magnitude multiplies it by $10^{-0.304} \approx 0.50$.

deeper.title: The university-exam analogy
deeper.body: The book compares the benchmarks to tests 'we like to give university students.' Imagine two students: one memorizes every past exam, the other understands the subject. On an exam built from questions like past exams, the first student's score rises steadily with how many past exams they memorize, a smooth 'scaling law'. Give both a problem unlike anything on past exams and the first student's memorized collection doesn't help. Scaling laws, on this view, measure how many past exams the model has memorized.

deeper.title: The three fundamental problems mapped to section 19.1
deeper.body:
| Bullet | What it says | Where it was argued |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Only interpolative programs memorized at training time; can't synthesize new ones at inference time | 19.1.1 (p.589-591): novel puzzles, Monty Hall variant |
| 2 | Poor generalization even in known situations: oversensitivity to phrasing and confounders | 19.1.2 (p.591-593): adversarial examples, Alice riddle, prompt engineering |
| 3 | Limited representational power: most programs aren't continuous morphings of a manifold | 19.1.3 (p.593): digit addition |

Scaling adds parameters and data to the same kind of model, so the book argues none of the three is addressed.

deeper.title: Where later chapters pick this up
deeper.body: The qualifier 'on their own, ... at inference time' in bullet 1 matters. The chapter later describes how, from 2024, test-time adaptation (search or fine-tuning during inference) led to major progress on ARC-AGI-1 at great computational cost (p.606, p.630), and argues that further conceptual advances such as combining deep learning with program synthesis are still needed (p.614).

visualizations.title: Why scaling doesn't fix the three problems
visualizations.why: Summarizes this page's argument: scaling improves memorization benchmarks, but the three fundamental problems in the bullet list stem from the unchanged curve-fitting paradigm.

misconceptions.claim: The book denies that scaling laws exist.
misconceptions.correction: It accepts the empirical relationship but argues that the benchmarks used are memorization tests, so the improvement reflects memorization, not progress on adaptation.

misconceptions.claim: Models four or five orders of magnitude larger must be qualitatively different.
misconceptions.correction: The book says they are 'still the same': parametric curves fitted via gradient descent using the Transformer architecture.

misconceptions.claim: More knowledgeable models are better at handling novel situations.
misconceptions.correction: The page distinguishes knowledge (more stored content) from the ability to synthesize new programs at inference time, which scaling hasn't provided.

takeaways: In early 2023, GPT-4's gains from scaling up GPT-3 fed the belief that more scaling would lead to AGI.
Scaling laws are real empirical relationships, but the book argues the benchmarks they use are memorization tests.

Scaling hasn't solved novelty, phrasing sensitivity or generalizable programs, because these are inherent to curve fitting, and the models are still parametric curves fitted by gradient descent with Transformers.
Three fundamental problems remain: only memorized interpolative programs; poor generalization with confounder sensitivity; limited representational power for algorithmic tasks.
19.2.1 begins the contrast between a differentiable parametric function and the human brain: automatons vs. intelligent agents.

questions.question: What is the book's main objection to using scaling laws as evidence that scale leads to general intelligence?
options: The benchmarks used to measure performance are effectively memorization tests
Larger models are too expensive to train
Scaling laws only apply to vision models
questions.answer: The benchmarks used to measure performance are effectively memorization tests
questions.explanation: The page says 'the benchmarks they're using to measure performance are effectively memorization tests.' The book does not call scaling laws invalid; cost is discussed in chapter 16 but is not the objection here; scaling laws are discussed for LLMs, not just vision.

questions.question: List the three fundamental problems that the book says scaling won't solve.
questions.answer: (1) Models are limited to interpolative programs memorized at training time and can't synthesize new programs at inference time for novel situations. (2) Even in known situations these programs generalize poorly, causing oversensitivity to phrasing and confounder features. (3) Models are limited in what they can represent: most programs, especially algorithmic reasoning, can't be expressed as a continuous geometric morphing of a data manifold.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets on the page; they restate 19.1.1, 19.1.2 and 19.1.3.

questions.question: Why does the book think four to five orders of magnitude of scaling made no progress on these problems?
questions.answer: Because the problems are inherent to curve fitting, and the models are still the same kind of thing: parametric curves fitted to a dataset by gradient descent, using the Transformer architecture. Scaling changes size and knowledge, not the paradigm.
questions.explanation: The page: 'We have not made any progress on these problems because the models we're using are still the same.'

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the issues the book says scaling has failed to address?
options: Inability to infer generalizable programs for reasoning problems
questions.explanation: The book lists the first three; it says models are now 'more knowledgeable', so knowledge has improved with scale. The point is that knowledge is not the same as adaptability.

questions.question: Suppose a scaling law gives loss $L \propto N^{-0.08}$. By what factor does the loss change if the model becomes 10,000 times larger? Does this, by itself, say anything about the three fundamental problems?
questions.answer: $10{,}000^{-0.08} = 10^{-0.32} \approx 0.48$: the loss roughly halves. By itself it says nothing about the three problems, since the loss measures fit to data like the training distribution.
questions.explanation: Power laws give predictable, diminishing improvements. The book's argument is about what is being measured: better fit to familiar data (memorization) doesn't imply adaptation to novelty. The formula is an AI-added illustration; the book gives none.

questions.question: According to the start of 19.2.1, what is the difference between humans and deep learning models beyond the fact that humans learn from embodied experience?
questions.answer: The human brain is 'an entirely different beast compared to a differentiable parametric function': humans do not simply apply a fixed geometric morphing from input to output.
questions.explanation: The book says the difference 'isn't just' embodiment; it's the nature of the system itself, which the following pages develop (automatons vs. intelligent agents, local vs. extreme generalization).

questions.question: Could you design a benchmark result that would convince the author that scaling had made progress on bullet 1? What property must the benchmark have?
questions.answer: It must test substantially novel tasks that can't be solved by memorized programs (e.g. new tasks not in any training data, like ARC puzzles), and a scaled-up model would need to improve on it without test-time search or special-casing.
questions.explanation: The book's critique is that standard benchmarks are memorization tests; a convincing benchmark must resist memorization, which is the design goal of ARC (p.605).
